findings.summary: Round one's install-after-close hole is genuinely closed, but close() still returns without waiting for an election already inside the store, so the hand-back of a term won in that window happens on the electing thread and is lost if the process exits first -- degrading a released lease into a TTL-bounded one.
findings.failure_scenario: A follower's commit is inside tryLead() (LocalSequencer.start: tryAcquire + the burned-epoch seals + recover(), latency unbounded in chain length). SIGTERM lands; close() sets closed=true, held.getAndSet(null) reads null, closes nothing and returns immediately, so the shutdown sequence believes the term is handed back. The election then wins epoch E, publishes to held, reads closed==true (the volatile-write-before-getAndSet ordering makes that read reliable -- the round-one defect is fixed), CASes held back to null and calls giveBack(won). If the JVM exits before that virtual thread returns from the store, LocalSequencer.close() -- and therefore LeaseManager.release() -- never runs, so the lease at epoch E stays unexpired: every other pod's tryAcquire returns empty and the cluster has no leader until the TTL lapses (~10 s, ADR-0007), which is exactly the difference Sequencer#close is specified to buy. Strictly bounded, unlike round one's permanent leak, hence minor. A terminal close would take electing with a bounded wait (BoundedLock.takeOrFail with the ttl bound, the same argument LeaseManager.release makes for using ttl rather than renewInterval) so the hand-back happens before close returns.
